text: How long is the Suez Canal, and between which two terminal ports does it run?
notes: 193.3 km (120.1 mi), from the northern terminus of Port Said to the southern terminus of Port Tewfik at Suez. Name-collision trap: the Panama Canal article opens with an 82-kilometre (51-mile) figure, so a careless engine cites the Panama doc for a real-but-wrong length.

text: When did Maersk vessels resume trans-Suez crossings after the Houthi attacks, and what monthly losses did Egypt attribute to those attacks?
notes: Join the Maersk doc (vessels returned in January 2026, with crossings by Maersk Sebarok and Maersk Denver) with the Suez Canal doc (President Sisi cited monthly losses of $800 million). Trap: the Maersk doc also says that as of 2010 all 83 Maersk tankers diverted via the Cape of Good Hope, a different diversion a decade earlier; and the Suez doc's $1 billion Ever Given damage figure is a separate event.

text: Which ship carried Malcom McLean's first container voyage in 1956, how many trailer vans did it carry, and where did it sail to?
notes: The SS Ideal X, a refitted tanker, carried 58 trailer vans from Newark, New Jersey to Houston, Texas on 26 April 1956. Trap: the same article names the Hakone Maru (1968, 752 TEU) as the first TEU container ship, which is a different 'first'.

text: On what date did Changi Airport begin commercial operations, and on what date was it officially opened?
notes: Commercial operations commenced 1 July 1981; the official opening came five months later on 29 December 1981. Trap: the Heathrow doc has a near-identical two-date structure for Terminal 5 (opened by the Queen on 14 March 2008, opened to the public 27 March 2008) and for the airport itself (25 March 1946), so a careless engine answers with a Heathrow date.

text: What did Heathrow Terminal 5 cost to build, and when did it open to the public?
notes: Built for 4.3 billion pounds; opened to the public on 27 March 2008 (opened by Queen Elizabeth II on 14 March 2008). Trap: Changi's Jewel and Terminal 5 costs sit in the Changi doc, and Heathrow's own 105 million pound Pier 6 figure invites the wrong number.

text: What are the dimensions of the new lock chambers built for the Panama Canal expansion?
notes: 427 m (1,400 ft) long, 55 m (180 ft) wide and 18.3 m (60 ft) deep. Trap: the original Panama locks are 33.5 metres (110 ft) wide, stated in the same article's lead, and the Suez Canal doc gives width 205 to 225 m, which is a canal width not a lock width - the Suez Canal has no locks at all.

text: What is the maximum beam of a ship allowed through the Suez Canal, and how does that compare with the beam allowed by the Panama Canal's new locks?
notes: Suez permits a maximum beam of 77.5 m (254 ft) under certain conditions; the Panama Canal's new locks allow a beam of up to 49 m (160 ft). Requires both canal docs. Trap: the Panama article's original-lock width of 33.5 m is the lock, not the permitted beam, and citing only the Suez doc's 'larger ships than the Panama Canal' sentence gives no Panama figure.

text: What range and typical passenger count does the Boeing 787-9 offer?
notes: 7,565 nmi (14,010 km; 8,706 mi) with 296 passengers; it entered service on 7 August 2014 with All Nippon Airways. Trap: the Airbus A350 doc gives the A350-900 an 8,500 nmi range and 300-350 passengers - the direct competitor and the classic wrong citation. Also do not substitute the 787-8's 7,305 nmi / 248 seats.

text: How much container throughput did the Port of Shanghai handle, and in what year did it become the world's busiest container port?
notes: Shanghai overtook Singapore in 2010 handling 29.05 million TEU, and handled 43.3 million TEU in 2019. An undated single figure is incomplete because the two figures are nine years apart. Trap: the Port of Rotterdam doc discusses TEU rankings for 2020 and 2017 and would be cited for a Shanghai figure it does not contain.

text: What was Maersk's annual revenue in its 2025 financial year, and how many people worked for the group that year?
notes: US$53.988 billion revenue; 108,160 employees worked for the group in the 2025 financial year (the lead also says more than 100,000 employees worldwide in 2025). Trap: the same article gives around 25,000 employees at Maersk Line in 2012 and 10,800 at Damco as of 2008; those are units and earlier years, so citing them is a recency error.

text: Does the Suez Canal use locks to raise and lower ships?
notes: No. It is an artificial sea-level waterway and, according to Alois Negrelli's plans, contained no locks, with seawater flowing freely through it. The correct answer asserts an absence. Trap: the Panama Canal doc is full of lock detail (Gatun, Pedro Miguel, Miraflores, Agua Clara, Cocoli); an engine that cites it is citing the wrong canal entirely.

text: Has the Airbus A350 fleet suffered any fatalities or hull losses in service?
notes: The A350 fleet has flown more than 15 million flight hours and carried more than 600 million passengers with no fatalities and one hull loss in an airport-safety-related incident. The answer must assert the absence of fatalities while still reporting the one hull loss. Trap: the Boeing 787 doc records the type's first fatal crash and hull loss, Air India Flight 171 on 12 June 2025 - citing that for the A350 is the collision failure this question targets.

text: Does the Airbus A350 use the lithium-ion main battery design that caused the Boeing 787 to be grounded?
notes: No: in light of the 787 Dreamliner battery problems, Airbus decided in February 2013 to revert from lithium-ion to the proven nickel-cadmium technology (though flight testing continued with lithium-ion, and from late 2015 some A350s flew Saft Li-ion batteries). Requires the 787 doc for the January 2013 FAA grounding and the A350 doc for the reversion. Trap: citing the 787 battery-fire passage as if it described the A350.

text: Was Sea-Land's 35-foot container adopted as one of the ISO standard container sizes?
notes: No - to McLean's frustration, Sea-Land's 35-foot container was not adopted as one of the standard container sizes, even though Sea-Land's corner-fitting design did become the standard. The answer asserts an absence. Trap: the article does list Matson's 24-foot and the US domestic 48 ft and 53 ft lengths, so an engine can easily cite a real standard-sizes sentence that does not support a 35-foot adoption.

text: How many runways does Heathrow Airport operate, and how many does Changi Airport operate?
notes: Heathrow now has only two parallel east-west runways (it had six in the 1950s and a third runway remains unbuilt); Changi has three operational runways, each 4 kilometres long. The Heathrow half is partly a negation: there is no third runway. Trap: the long Heathrow third-runway narrative (Commons vote 415-119, Court of Appeal ruling, Supreme Court lifting the ban in December 2020) tempts an engine into saying Heathrow has three.

text: How many ships per day is the Panama Canal currently allowing to transit, and how does that compare with normal operations?
notes: In normal times 36 ships per day; from 3 September 2026 only 34, and from 15 September 2026 the number dropped to 32 amid low rainfall and an intensifying El Nino. An undated answer is incomplete because the article also gives 22 per day in early December 2023 and 24 per day in January 2024. Trap: citing the 2023 drought figure as current, or citing the Suez doc's 49-to-97 ships per day capacity figures.

text: How many orders and deliveries has the Boeing 787 programme recorded?
notes: As of August 2026 the 787 programme had received 2,466 orders and made 1,303 deliveries. The figures must be dated. Trap: the Airbus A350 doc gives 1,624 ordered and 734 delivered as of the same month, which is the obvious wrong-aircraft citation.

text: Which airline is the largest operator of the Airbus A350, and how many of the aircraft does it have?
notes: As of August 2026, Singapore Airlines is the largest operator with 65 aircraft in its fleet (Turkish Airlines is the largest customer, with 110 on order). The 'as of' date is required because the article's fleet totals are explicitly dated. Trap: the 787 doc names All Nippon Airways and Singapore Airlines as launch/entry-into-service operators of 787 variants, so an engine can cite the wrong aircraft while naming a real airline.

text: How many passengers did Changi Airport handle in 2025, and how did that compare with the previous year?
notes: 69,980,000 passengers for the 2025 full year, a 3.4% increase compared to 2024 and the highest in its 44-year history. Trap: Heathrow's busiest year ever was 2024 with 83.9 million passengers - a bigger, real, differently-sourced number from the collision document. Also avoid Changi's own 'about 70 million' rounding without the year.

text: How many locomotives does Union Pacific have on its roster?
notes: The article's lead says Union Pacific operates 8,300 locomotives, but it also states that as of December 2023 the active roster held 7,175 locomotives across 42 models, and gives 8,721 at the end of 2007 and nearly 7,000 as of 1999. The figures disagree and are differently dated; a single undated number is partial. Trap: treating the lead's 8,300 as the current roster without noting the dated 7,175.

text: By how much did the Panama Canal expansion increase the canal's shipping capacity?
notes: The article states both that the expansion proposal was expected to double the canal's shipping capacity and that the completed 2016 expansion nearly tripled its previous capacity. The disagreement within the source is the fact; a single figure citing one sentence is partial. Trap: the Suez doc's 'nearly double the capacity, from 49 to 97 ships per day' is the wrong canal with a confusingly similar claim.

text: What did it cost to develop the Airbus A350?
notes: Estimates disagree: the XWB redesign raised development costs from US$5.5 billion to approximately US$10 billion; Reuters estimated the total at US$15 billion (EUR 12 billion); and in June 2013 costs were estimated at EUR 11 billion. Earlier figures of EUR 4 billion committed and around EUR 3.5 billion at industrial launch also appear. A single figure is partial. Trap: the Boeing 787 doc's $32 billion programme spend is the wrong aircraft.

text: How many Boeing 787 sales are needed for the programme to break even, and how much has Boeing spent on it?
notes: Boeing has spent $32 billion on the programme, and estimates for the number of aircraft sales needed to break even vary between 1,300 and 2,000. The spread is the fact; quoting one end as the break-even point is partial. Trap: the A350 doc's unit costs ($317.4m and $366.5m in 2018) and its development-cost estimates invite a wrong-aircraft citation.

text: Where does the Port of Rotterdam rank among the world's ports?
notes: The article gives several incompatible rankings: largest seaport in Europe and the world's largest outside Asia; world's busiest by annual cargo tonnage from 1962 until 2004; the world's tenth-largest container port by TEU in 2020; the world's tenth-largest cargo port by tonnage in 2017; and a closing line calling Rotterdam the sixth biggest port in the world. The conflict and the dates are the fact. Trap: the Port of Shanghai doc's 'world's busiest container port' claim is a different port.
aspects: sixth biggest port in the world

text: How busy is Changi Airport in global rankings, according to its 2025 figures?
notes: The article gives conflicting 2025 rankings: as of 2025 Changi ranked 16th busiest airport by passenger traffic and 4th busiest international airport by seat volume on OAG's records, while the airport's own 2025 full-year figures make it the fourth busiest international airport in the world and the seventh busiest in Asia Pacific. Both must be reported. Trap: Heathrow's 2025 claims (busiest in Europe, fifth-busiest in the world, second-busiest by international passenger traffic) are the neighbouring document and a very easy mis-citation.

text: What container capacity is reported for the Emma Maersk, and what claim is made about its size?
notes: The Containerization article says some ships can carry over 14,500 TEU, 'such as the Emma Maersk, 396 m long, launched in August 2006'; the Maersk article calls the Emma Maersk the largest container ship in the world to that date, delivered in 2006, and notes Maersk then ordered the even larger Triple E class at 18,000 containers each. The capacity claims differ and the 'largest' claim is time-bounded. Trap: quoting the Triple E's 18,000 as Emma Maersk's capacity.
aspects: largest container ship in the world

text: Which Maersk business unit operates container terminals at Rotterdam, and what kind of area is Maasvlakte?
notes: Maersk's APM Terminals unit (headquartered in The Hague, interests in 57 ports in 36 countries) lists Rotterdam-Maasvlakte and Rotterdam-Maasvlakte 2 among its European terminals; the Port of Rotterdam doc describes Maasvlakte as reclaimed land projecting into the North Sea, completed in the 1970s, with a second Maasvlakte approved in 2006. Requires both docs. Trap: Europe Container Terminals runs the automated Delta and Euromax terminals at Rotterdam and is not a Maersk unit, so citing the robotic-cranes passage answers the wrong question.

text: Which Airbus A350 variant flew the record-setting flight out of Singapore Changi in October 2018, where did it land, and how long did it take?
notes: The A350-900ULR, operated by Singapore Airlines, landed the world's then-longest flight at Newark Liberty International Airport from Singapore Changi on 12 October 2018 after 17 hours and 52 minutes. Joins the A350 doc with the Changi doc (Changi as Singapore Airlines' home base and the airport in question). Trap: the Boeing 787 doc's Singapore Airlines link is the 787-10's entry into service on 3 April 2018 - same airline, same year, wrong aircraft and wrong event.
